en: An open insult; to insult intentionally
hook: AFFRONT: an insult right to your FRONT, to your face.
story: Affront. At a family wedding, Tanvir's elderly uncle was seated at the very back, behind the cooks, while younger relatives sat at the head table. He took it as a deliberate insult and left before dinner was served. He called it an affront: an open, intentional insult. As a verb, to affront someone is to insult them openly. The root means to the face, so an affront is an insult thrown right in your face. Synonyms: insult, slight, outrage.

gre.s: The ambassador regarded the decision to seat him behind junior officials as a deliberate ____, a public insult to his country that demanded a formal apology.
gre.clue: a public insult to his country that demanded a formal apology

example: Being left off the guest list for her cousin's wedding felt like an affront to Nasrin, who had helped plan every detail of the engagement.

en: Telling a story whose characters and events stand for deeper ideas
hook: ALLEGORICAL: ALL the story is a symbol for something else.
story: Allegorical. In an English literature class in Dhaka, students read Animal Farm. On the surface, it is a story about pigs and horses who take over a farm. But every animal stands for something: the pigs for power hungry leaders, the loyal horse for the working class, the sheep for people who repeat slogans. The story is allegorical: using symbols to convey a hidden moral or political meaning. An allegory says one thing on the surface and means another beneath. Synonyms: symbolic, figurative.

gre.s: Readers who take the fable literally miss its point; its talking animals are plainly ____, each standing for a faction in the political struggles of the author's day.
gre.clue: each standing for a faction

example: Visitors to the gallery debated whether the painter's sinking boat was allegorical or just a memory of a real ferry accident.

en: Open and willing to be persuaded or to cooperate
hook: AMENABLE: says 'AMEN' readily, agreeing to your suggestion.
story: Amenable. Mitu rehearsed for a whole week. She had arguments, statistics, and a backup plan, all to convince her strict father to let her study abroad. She sat him down, took a deep breath, and began. Two minutes later, he said, "Fine. Which university?" She stared at him. He had been amenable all along: open to suggestion and easy to persuade. An amenable person listens and cooperates. Think of someone who quickly says amen to your idea.

gre.s: Although the director was initially stubborn about the ending, she proved ____ to suggestions once the test audiences reacted poorly.
gre.clue: Although the director was initially stubborn

example: The landlord proved amenable to a lower rent once Tania offered to repaint the flat herself.

en: Cleverly skilled, often at tricking or manipulating others
hook: ARTFUL: full of the ART of tricks — the opposite of artless.
story: Artful. Every evening at the Sadarghat launch terminal, a boy named Babu sold peanuts to passengers. When the guards chased hawkers away, Babu simply put on a school cap, opened a book, and pretended to wait for his father, selling quietly from his schoolbag. The guards never caught on. Babu was artful: clever and skillful, often in a sly, crafty way. Charles Dickens named a young pickpocket the Artful Dodger. An artful answer dodges a question gracefully. Synonyms: cunning, wily.

gre.s: The senator's ____ evasions impressed even her opponents: she could sidestep a damaging question so smoothly that reporters rarely noticed it had gone unanswered.
gre.clue: so smoothly that reporters rarely noticed it had gone unanswered

example: With an artful bit of flattery, the young salesman persuaded my grandmother to buy two pressure cookers she never needed.

en: So common and unoriginal that it is boring
hook: BANAL: as boring as a BANANA, which you've eaten a thousand times.
story: Banal. Arif's GRE essay began: "Since the dawn of time, humans have always…" His tutor put down her pen and sighed. "Arif, half of all students start exactly this way. The examiner has read this sentence a thousand times today." Banal means so common and overused that it has become boring and empty. Banal small talk, banal song lyrics, banal advice like "just be yourself." To impress examiners, avoid the banal and say something fresh.

gre.s: Though the speech was praised for its delivery, its content was ____, a string of platitudes the audience had heard countless times.
gre.clue: a string of platitudes the audience had heard countless times

example: The song's lyrics were so banal, rhyming 'heart' with 'apart' in every verse, that the judges eliminated it in the first round.

en: To talk about someone or something as if they hardly matter
hook: BE-LITTLE: make it LITTLE.
story: Belittle. Shuvo spent two weeks building a small solar lamp for the school science fair. His older brother glanced at it and laughed. "Anyone can make that by watching one video online." Shuvo's excitement drained away. His brother had belittled his effort: made it seem small and unimportant. The word is easy to remember: be little, to make something little. Good teachers never belittle a student's question, however simple. Synonyms: disparage, deprecate, diminish.

gre.s: Insecure about his own modest achievements, the manager tended to ____ the accomplishments of his subordinates, dismissing even their major successes as mere luck.
gre.clue: dismissing even their major successes as mere luck

example: A good coach never belittles a nervous swimmer after a false start, because shame rarely makes anyone faster.

en: Loud, lively, and full of high spirits, sometimes unruly
hook: BOISTEROUS: BOYS-terous, a room full of loud, playful boys.
story: Boisterous. On Eid morning, Grandma's house fills with twenty cousins. They race up and down the stairs, shout across rooms, wrestle on the sofa, and play cricket in the hallway with a rolled-up newspaper. A vase wobbles; an uncle shouts; everyone laughs louder. Nobody can hear the TV. The cousins are boisterous: noisy, energetic, and cheerful, a little rowdy. Boisterous crowds celebrate loudly. Picture a room full of boys being boys.

gre.s: The usually ____ classroom fell completely silent when the principal walked in unannounced.
gre.clue: fell completely silent

example: The boisterous cousins turned the wedding's quiet garden into a cricket pitch until an aunt confiscated the ball.

en: Shrewd and careful, especially in money or business matters
hook: CANNY: like a CAN-do person who's never fooled.
story: Canny. Joya's grandmother is the most canny shopper in Kawran Bazar. She checks every tomato, knows the fair price of everything, notices when the scale is tilted, and bargains so skilfully that vendors lower their prices just to end the conversation. She has never been cheated in fifty years. She is canny: shrewd and careful, especially with money. Careful: uncanny means strange and mysterious, a completely different word.

gre.s: A ____ negotiator, she waited until the seller grew desperate before making her offer, securing the property far below its asking price.
gre.clue: waited until the seller grew desperate before making her offer

example: Canny shoppers at New Market know to walk away once while bargaining, since the seller usually calls them back with a lower price.

en: Frustration mixed with embarrassment after a failure or humiliation
hook: CHAGRIN: you wanted to GRIN, but SHAME (cha) took over.
story: Chagrin. Farhan told all his friends that he would top the class in the final exam. When the results came out, he had failed one subject, and his quiet roommate had come first. Farhan's face burned with chagrin: annoyance and distress caused by humiliation or failure. It often appears as, much to his chagrin. Chagrin is not plain sadness; it is the sting of embarrassment. Despite the sound, there is no grin in it. Synonyms: mortification, vexation.

gre.s: Much to the general's ____, the battle he had boasted would last a single afternoon dragged on for months, exposing his strategy as hopelessly naive.
gre.clue: he had boasted would last a single afternoon

example: To the chef's chagrin, the visiting food critic sent back the biryani because the rice was undercooked.

en: An expert judge in matters of taste, especially art, food, or drink
hook: CONNOISSEUR: 'connaître' is French for 'to know'. One who really knows.
story: Connoisseur. Uncle Mamun takes one bite of biryani and closes his eyes. "Basmati, aged two years. Mutton marinated overnight. A little too much nutmeg. This is from Haji, not Fakhruddin." He is always right. Restaurant owners in Old Dhaka fear and respect him. Uncle Mamun is a connoisseur: an expert judge in matters of taste, especially food, art, music, or wine. The French verb connaître means to know. A connoisseur does not just enjoy; he judges.

gre.s: Only a true ____ of early jazz could distinguish the original recordings from the expert imitations that flooded the market in the 1950s.
gre.clue: could distinguish the original recordings from the expert imitations

example: A connoisseur of handloom saris, Shahana can tell a genuine Jamdani from a machine copy by running a fingertip over the weave.

en: Behavior that is polite, proper, and appropriate to the situation
hook: DECORUM is related to DECORATE: decent, proper presentation.
story: Decorum. At the funeral, everyone spoke softly and dressed in white. Prayers drifted through the courtyard. Then a phone blared loud dance music, and its owner laughed as he fumbled to silence it. Every elder in the room turned and glared. He had broken decorum: the polite, dignified behaviour expected in a situation. Courtrooms, exam halls, mosques, and wedding stages all have their own rules of decorum. Breaking them is a social crime.

gre.s: The senator was censured for violating the chamber's ____, having shouted insults at a colleague during a solemn debate.
gre.clue: having shouted insults at a colleague

example: The memorial service was conducted with quiet decorum until a phone with a loud ringtone went off in the front row.

en: Quick and skillful, especially with the hands
hook: DEFT sounds like the opposite of DAFT: not stupid, but skilled.
story: Deft. Outside Farhan's office, a street vendor makes parathas all evening. Flip, flip, crack an egg, sprinkle onions, fold, wrap in paper, hand it over, take the money, give change, all in about ten seconds, without looking down once. Crowds gather just to watch his hands. He is deft: quick, neat, and skilful, especially with the hands. A deft politician handles hard questions smoothly; a deft surgeon never wastes a movement.

gre.s: The diplomat's ____ handling of the dispute, defusing it with a single well-chosen compromise, earned praise from both sides.
gre.clue: defusing it with a single well-chosen compromise

example: With a few deft strokes of the brush, the rickshaw painter added a tiger to the back panel in under five minutes.

en: Deep moral rottenness; extreme wickedness
hook: DEPRAVITY: DEPRIVED of all goodness.
story: Depravity. The detective novel Shuvo was reading described a villain who poisoned his own brother for an inheritance, then framed a loyal servant and smiled as the innocent man was led away. Shuvo put the book down, disturbed by such depravity: moral corruption, wickedness. Depraved comes from the Latin pravus, meaning crooked; a depraved person is morally twisted. Do not confuse it with deprivation, which means lacking necessities. Synonyms: wickedness, corruption, vice, degeneracy.

gre.s: The prosecutor described the crimes as acts of shocking ____, committed not out of desperation but out of sheer delight in the suffering of others.
gre.clue: sheer delight in the suffering of others

example: The novel traces a gifted student's slow slide into depravity, from small lies to cheating and finally to blackmail.

en: Excessively harsh and severe, especially of laws
hook: DRACONIAN: from DRACO, an ancient Greek lawmaker who gave the death penalty for small crimes.
story: Draconian. A new hostel warden announced his rules: lights out at nine, no visitors ever, phones confiscated every night, and any student who returned even one minute late would be expelled. The students called the rules draconian: excessively harsh and severe. The word comes from Draco, a lawmaker in ancient Athens whose laws punished even petty theft with death. It was said his laws were written not in ink but in blood. Synonyms: harsh, severe, punitive, oppressive.

gre.s: Critics condemned the law as ____, pointing out that it imposed ten year prison sentences for offenses as trivial as littering.
gre.clue: ten year prison sentences for offenses as trivial as littering

example: The company's draconian attendance policy docked a full day's pay from any worker who arrived even five minutes late.

en: To invent something false in order to deceive; to construct
hook: FABRICATE: FABRIC of lies, stitched together.
story: Fabricate. Khalid missed the deadline for his research paper. To cover it up, he told his supervisor that his laptop had been stolen, invented a police report number, and even described the thief. None of it was true. He had fabricated the story: invented something false in order to deceive. Fabricate can also simply mean to construct, as in fabricating steel parts in a factory. On the GRE, it usually means to make up. Synonyms: concoct, invent, falsify.

gre.s: The journalist was dismissed after editors discovered that she had chosen to ____ several quotations, attributing to real officials words they had never spoken.
gre.clue: attributing to real officials words they had never spoken

example: Investigators found that the lab had fabricated data for at least four published studies, and the journal retracted all of them.

en: Unfortunate; unlucky
hook: HAP-LESS: without HAPpiness or luck (hap = luck).
story: Hapless. Poor Sabbir. On the day of his job interview, his rickshaw got a flat tire, the rain soaked his only suit, he stepped into an open drain, and he finally arrived to learn that the interview had been held the day before. His friends could not decide whether to laugh or cry for him. He was hapless: unfortunate, unlucky. Hap is an old word for luck, as in happen and perhaps; hapless means without luck. Synonyms: unlucky, luckless, ill fated.

gre.s: The ____ explorer seemed cursed: his ship sank, his supplies were stolen, and when he finally reached the coast, he found it already claimed by a rival.
gre.clue: seemed cursed

example: The hapless goalkeeper slipped on the wet grass twice in the same match, gifting the visitors both of their goals.

en: Not allowing fluid to pass through; unaffected by
hook: IMPERVIOUS: nothing gets through, waterproof to water or criticism.
story: Impervious. Before the monsoon, Mitu bought a good raincoat. Under the heaviest downpour on the way to class, the rain beaded and rolled off; not a single drop got through. The coat was impervious to water. Her professor, meanwhile, seems impervious to criticism: no complaint ever affects him. Impervious means not letting fluid pass through, or not affected by something. The Latin root means no way through. Synonyms: impermeable, unaffected, immune.

gre.s: So convinced was the director of her own vision that she seemed ____ to criticism, continuing to film exactly as she had planned despite the producers' increasingly anxious notes.
gre.clue: continuing to film exactly as she had planned

example: Seemingly impervious to the heat, the old farmer kept planting seedlings through the noon sun while his sons rested in the shade.

en: Angry at something unjust
hook: INDIGNANT: your DIGNITY was insulted.
story: Indignant. At a government office, Rahim waited four hours in line to renew his passport. Then a man in a suit walked straight to the counter, slipped the clerk an envelope, and was served at once. Rahim was indignant: angry at something unjust. He stood up and demanded to know why bribes came before citizens. Indignant comes from the Latin for unworthy; we feel indignant when something unworthy is done. Indignation is righteous anger. Synonyms: outraged, aggrieved, incensed.

gre.s: Accused of a theft she had not committed, the housekeeper was not frightened but ____, demanding an apology from the family that had wrongly suspected her.
gre.clue: a theft she had not committed

example: Passengers grew indignant when the bus company doubled its fares overnight, without any notice, just before Eid.

en: The lowest point
hook: NADIR: the opposite of zenith, the bottom of everything.
story: Nadir. The year Arif's father lost his business, the family sold their car, moved into a single rented room, and Arif nearly dropped out of school. That winter was the nadir of their lives: the lowest point. Slowly, things improved. In astronomy, the nadir is the point directly below an observer, opposite the zenith overhead. Both words come from Arabic. Remember: nadir is down, zenith is up. Synonyms: low point, rock bottom.

gre.s: The team's season reached its ____ in March, when a string of humiliating defeats left it in last place; only then did its slow recovery begin.
gre.clue: a string of humiliating defeats left it in last place

example: Relations between the two sisters hit their nadir when they argued over their mother's house and stopped speaking for a year.

en: Small or meager; worthless
hook: PALTRY: like a PALTRY chicken — PALLID and puny.
story: Paltry. After a month of twelve-hour shifts at a garment factory in Gazipur, Rumana opened her pay envelope to find a sum that barely covered her rent. Her Eid bonus was even smaller, just enough for a pair of sandals. It was a paltry amount: small, meagre, almost worthless. Paltry can also describe a weak excuse or a feeble effort. Think of poultry feed: a tiny handful of grain. Synonyms: meagre, trifling, measly.

gre.s: Despite the company's record profits, the raise it offered its workers was ____, amounting to less than the price of a cup of tea per day.
gre.clue: amounting to less than the price of a cup of tea per day

example: After three months of selling handmade candles, Rumana had earned a paltry five hundred taka, barely enough to cover the wax.

en: Seemingly contradictory but possibly true
hook: PARADOX: two contradictory things that are both true.
story: Paradoxical. Ishrat's doctor told her something strange: to cure her constant tiredness, she should exercise more. How could spending energy give her more energy? Yet after a month of morning walks, she felt less tired than ever. The advice was paradoxical: seemingly contradictory, but possibly true. A paradox looks impossible but holds a truth, like less is more. Para means against, and dox means opinion, as in orthodox: a paradox goes against expectation. Synonyms: contradictory, counterintuitive.

gre.s: It may seem ____ that adding new roads can worsen traffic, yet studies show that extra lanes often attract so many new drivers that congestion increases.
gre.clue: yet studies show

example: It seems paradoxical that the busiest people often reply to emails fastest, yet they usually have the most practiced routines.

en: Slowly and quietly causing serious harm or damage
hook: PERNICIOUS: slowly PERISHING you.
story: Pernicious. Rafi started checking his phone for just a minute before studying. A month later, that minute had become three hours a night, his grades had slipped, and he could not read a page without reaching for the screen. The habit never seemed dangerous on any single day; its harm grew quietly. It was pernicious: harmful, especially in a gradual or subtle way. Noxious harm is obvious, like poison gas; pernicious harm creeps in unnoticed. Synonyms: insidious, destructive.

gre.s: The rumors were all the more ____ for being subtle: no single falsehood seemed serious, yet together they slowly destroyed public trust in the institution.
gre.clue: yet together they slowly destroyed public trust

example: Constant comparison on social media can have a pernicious effect on teenagers, eroding their confidence a little each day.

en: Developing skills or maturity much earlier than is usual
hook: PRE-COCIOUS: PRE-COOKED early, ripe too soon.
story: Precocious. Mahin was four years old when he began reading his father's newspaper aloud at breakfast. By seven, he was solving his sister's high school math problems and asking his teacher about black holes. Relatives called him precocious: showing unusually early development, especially mental. The word comes from the Latin for ripened early, like fruit that ripens before its season. A precocious child seems older than his years. Synonyms: advanced, forward, gifted.

gre.s: Remarkably ____, the boy was reading novels at three and solving algebra problems at six, years before most of his peers could do either.
gre.clue: years before most of his peers could do either

example: A precocious violinist, Arnob joined the city orchestra at eleven and played his first solo concert at Shilpakala Academy a year later.

en: High-pitched and piercing; loud and forceful in criticism
hook: SHRILL: like a SHRIEKING whistle.
story: Shrill. In Babu's flat, the pressure cooker whistle pierced the air, and a moment later his little sister shrieked at the cat. Both sounds were shrill: high-pitched and piercing. Shrill also describes criticism that is loud and forceful, often too forceful. One newspaper attacked the minister in shrill editorials every single day, until readers stopped listening. Say the word aloud and you can hear its sharp, whistling sound. Synonyms: piercing, strident.

gre.s: The opposition's attacks grew increasingly ____, so loud and relentless that even sympathetic voters began to dismiss them as hysteria rather than reasoned argument.
gre.clue: so loud and relentless

example: The kettle's shrill whistle woke the whole household before dawn, ending any hope Raju had of sleeping late.

en: To calm down or ease off after being intense or severe
hook: SUB-SIDE: sinking down (sub) to the side.
story: Subside. The fever started on Monday night. Lamia's temperature climbed to a hundred and three, and her mother sat beside her with wet cloths until dawn. By Wednesday the fever began to subside, and by Friday Lamia was hungry again. To subside is to become less intense, violent, or severe. Floods subside, anger subsides, and noise subsides. Sub means under and sid means settle: things sink back down. Synonyms: abate, recede, diminish.

gre.s: The villagers camped on the embankment for three days, waiting for the floodwaters to ____ so that they could return and inspect their damaged homes.
gre.clue: so that they could return and inspect their damaged homes

example: Once the fever began to subside, the doctor allowed Mitu to eat a little rice and lentil soup.

en: Bending and moving easily; flexible
hook: SUPPLE: as soft and flexible as SUPPLE leather.
story: Supple. Shathi has practised classical dance since she was five. She can bend backward until her palms touch the floor and twist her wrists into shapes that make audiences gasp. Her body is supple: bending and moving easily, flexible. Good leather is supple, soft and pliable. A supple mind adapts quickly to new ideas. Say supple aloud, and it even sounds soft and springy. Synonyms: flexible, pliant, lithe, limber. Opposites: stiff, rigid.

gre.s: Years of daily yoga had kept the old man remarkably ____: at eighty, he could still bend easily enough to touch his toes.
gre.clue: he could still bend easily enough to touch his toes

example: Soaked overnight in water, dry cane becomes supple enough for basket weavers in Sylhet to bend it into tight circles.

en: An extended, furious outburst that attacks someone or something
hook: TIRADE: so long it TIRES everyone out.
story: Tirade. When the bus conductor overcharged him by ten taka, a passenger began shouting, and did not stop. For fifteen minutes he attacked the conductor, the bus company, the traffic police, and the state of the nation, while everyone stared out of the windows. It was a tirade: a long, angry speech of criticism. Think of a tirade as a tiring rant that never ends. Synonyms: diatribe, harangue, rant, broadside. Opposites: eulogy and panegyric, speeches of praise.

gre.s: Instead of offering constructive feedback, the critic launched into a furious ____ against the novel, denouncing its plot, its characters, and its author for nearly ten pages.
gre.clue: denouncing its plot, its characters, and its author for nearly ten pages

example: The taxi driver's tirade against the city's potholes lasted the entire forty-minute ride from Uttara to Motijheel.

en: An act that violates a rule, law, or moral code
hook: TRANS-GRESS: stepping ACROSS (trans) the line.
story: Transgression. The national team's best bowler was caught on camera scratching the ball with a bottle cap to make it swing. He apologized and cried at the press conference, but the cricket board banned him for a full year. His transgression shocked fans who had idolized him. A transgression is an act that violates a rule, law, or moral code. Trans means across, gress means step: stepping across the line. Small transgressions can grow into big ones.

gre.s: The senator's minor ____, a forgotten parking fine, was seized upon by opponents eager to portray him as contemptuous of the law.
gre.clue: a forgotten parking fine

example: Under the boarding school's strict code, even reading a novel after lights-out counted as a serious transgression.

en: Hidden beyond what is obvious, usually a selfish motive
hook: ULTERIOR: the motive lies ULTERIOR, further beyond.
story: Ulterior. Tania's classmate, who had ignored her for three years, suddenly began bringing her tea, praising her notes, and inviting her to lunch. Two weeks before exams, he asked to borrow all her notes. Tania realised that his sudden friendship had an ulterior motive: a hidden, selfish purpose beyond what was obvious. Ulterior comes from the Latin for further or beyond. It almost always appears with the word motive. Synonyms: hidden, concealed, covert.

gre.s: Though the billionaire insisted that his donation was purely charitable, skeptics suspected that he had ____ motives, noting that it was announced just before his trial began.
gre.clue: announced just before his trial began

example: Rana's sudden offer to wash his sister's car made her wonder what ulterior purpose lay behind such unusual kindness.

en: Extremely damaging or infectious; full of bitter hatred
hook: VIRULENT: like a VIRUS, spreading poison.
story: Virulent. In one cold season, a new strain of influenza spread through Dhaka's hostels. It was virulent: it spread rapidly and caused severe illness, sending dozens of students to hospital. Online, arguments about the outbreak became virulent too, full of insults and hatred. Virulent means extremely harmful or poisonous, or bitterly hostile. Think of a virus spreading poison. Virulent criticism is vicious and venomous.

gre.s: The pamphlet's ____ attacks on the minority community, full of hateful slurs, led to its immediate ban.
gre.clue: full of hateful slurs

example: Public health officers in Chattogram tracked a virulent strain of cholera that spread through three neighborhoods within a week.
